compare.title: Desktop Commander is #1. {product} gives your AI the whole secure space.
compare.intro: Desktop Commander puts a computer in the chat. {product} is built for everything around that: every machine you have, a hub you own, and you in the loop. Side by side, from Desktop Commander's own source. Each § opens its evidence.

rows.them: Desktop Commander's own service. Its server is not in the open repository.
rows.us: You do, with one Docker command. Or use the hosted hub.
evidence: Remote MCP goes through Desktop Commander's hosted service, `mcp.desktopcommander.app` by default (`src/remote-device/device.ts:104`).

Not in the repository at that commit: the Remote MCP server that ChatGPT and Claude connect to and its OAuth, the device sign-in endpoints, the dashboard, and the database schema and policies. The teardown searched `src/`, `scripts/` and `test/` for them.

source.label: Read the section in the teardown

rows.them: Each call's arguments and its result sit in a row of their cloud database (Supabase) until it is swept.
rows.us: From your hub straight down the machine's own link. The hub stores neither arguments nor output.
evidence: A call is a row in the `mcp_remote_calls` table of a Supabase Postgres database. The device claims the row, runs the call, and writes the result back into the same row (`src/remote-device/remote-channel.ts:912-1004`, `:1269-1321`).

Its README says the service stores tool arguments and results there temporarily, and sweeps finished rows at least a minute after they complete (`src/remote-device/README.md:220`). The service's side of this is not in the repository, so the teardown marks those steps INFERRED.

source.label: Read the section in the teardown

rows.them: Tokens in a file, device.json. A copy of the file is the device.
rows.us: Its own Ed25519 key, proved over a fresh challenge every time it connects.
evidence: `desktop-commander remote` keeps its access and refresh tokens in `~/.desktop-commander-device/device.json`, written with mode 0600 (`src/remote-device/device.ts:40-59`, `:466-503`). Keeping the session is on by default (`src/remote-device/device.ts:109-113`).
The plan's §14 sums it up: there is no device key, so a copied `device.json` is the whole account.

source.label: Read the section in the teardown

rows.us: Your AI asks, and you approve or deny on your phone.
evidence: The plan's §14, from the teardown: no approval before a command. A call the device claims from its queue goes to the local server and runs (`src/remote-device/device.ts:600-694`, teardown §3.7).

rows.them: Anything but 34 blocked names, matched on each command's first word. The AI can change the list itself.
rows.us: Each machine decides: only the programs you granted, or what its own account may. On Linux that is a service account, never root.
evidence: The default `blockedCommands` list has 34 names, from `mkfs` and `sudo` to `shutdown` (`src/config-manager.ts:233-277`). The check splits a command line on `;`, `&&`, `||`, `|` and `&` and matches the first word of each part (`src/command-manager.ts:16-267`).

The model can rewrite the list with `set_config_value`; the only guard is a note in that tool's description (`src/server.ts:339-365`). From reading the parser (INFERRED, not run): a newline is not a separator, and `bash -c "…"` hides what it runs.

source.label: Read the section in the teardown

rows.them: Log files on the machine with every call's full arguments, rotated at 10 MB.
rows.us: An append-only, {term:audit} on the hub. A call it cannot record is refused.
evidence: Every call's arguments go unredacted to `claude_tool_call.log`, rotated at 10 MB with the rotated files kept, and calls with their results to `tool-history.jsonl`, capped at 1000 records (`src/config.ts:10-11`, `src/utils/toolHistory.ts:55-74`). The teardown files them as local audit trails, not boundaries.

source.label: Read the section in the teardown

rows.them: Processes tracked by OS PID. A single wait is capped at 50 seconds.
rows.us: The machine's broker owns each job. It outlives the AI's connection; disconnecting never stops it.
evidence: Terminal sessions live in a map keyed by OS PID (`src/terminal-manager.ts:114-144`). Any single blocking wait is capped at `MAX_PROCESS_WAIT_MS = 50000`, to stay under the MCP SDK's 60-second request timeout (`src/config.ts:13-23`).

source.label: Read the section in the teardown

rows.them: On by default. Install and setup send events without checking the opt-out.
evidence: `telemetryEnabled` defaults to `true` (`src/config-manager.ts:280`). The npm `postinstall` script sends a `package_installed` event, and the `setup` command about thirty `npx_setup_*` events, neither checking the opt-out (`track-installation.js:43-78`, `setup-claude-server.js:14-27`).

source.label: Read the section in the teardown

rows.them: No shared board among its 25 tools.
rows.us: A ticket board the agents share: claim, notes, handoff.
evidence: `tools/list` advertises 25 tools (`src/server.ts:306-1158`): configuration, files, search, processes, PDFs and feedback. None of them is a board or queue that several agents share.

source.label: Read the section in the teardown

evidence: `package.json` requires Node.js 22.12.0 or later, and its `install.sh` enforces the same (`package.json:15-17`, `install.sh:22-24`).

source.label: Read the section in the teardown

rows.them: Free up to 10,000 remote tool calls a month, then $20 a month.
rows.us: Self-hosted: no limit on calls. Hosted: free during the alpha.
evidence: Its pricing page, read on 1 November 2026: Free, $0 a month with 10,000 tool calls a month; Pro, $20 a month with unlimited tool calls. The local server is free and open source. Nothing in the repository counts calls, so the teardown infers the cap is metered on Remote MCP calls by the hosted service.

Claude and Codex coordinate on one ticket board: claim work, leave notes, hand off.
A Docker image and compose with its own Postgres, claimed from your browser with the code from its log. Or the same hub, hosted at {domain}.
Each machine runs a {term:broker} that owns its jobs and a {term:link} that dials out to the hub. Nothing on the machine listens on the network.

self_host.title: Self-host with one command
self_host.intro: On any Linux box with Docker: name your hub once, then one command brings up the hub, its own Postgres and Caddy for TLS.
terminal: # once: get it and name your hub
facts: Claim it in your browser with the {term:claim-code} from its log: `docker compose logs hub`. {pop:claim|How claiming works}
Postgres has no network at all. The hub reaches it over a Unix socket, so there is no database password to keep.
Caddy gets the certificate for your domain.

On a Debian or Ubuntu server, `install.sh` does all of this and keeps the hub current: it pins the image by its {term:digest}, deploys each new one after a backup, and keeps it only if the hub comes up healthy. The database is backed up nightly too.
GitHub builds the image for x86_64 and ARM64 from every commit on main, with signed build provenance you can check.
self_host.hosted: Rather not run it? Use the same hub hosted at {domain}, free during the alpha: your account there is made the first time your AI connects.

faq.title: Questions

questions.q: Is {product} a fork of Desktop Commander?
questions.a: No. It is written from scratch in Rust to replace it: a broker on each machine that owns its jobs, a thin MCP adapter, and the hub between them and your AI.

questions.q: Does anything on my machine accept connections?
questions.a: No. The machine's link opens one outbound WebSocket to the hub and keeps it. No port opens on the machine, so it works behind any router or firewall.

questions.q: What can my AI do on a machine?
questions.a: Start programs as jobs and read their output; read, write and edit files; list folders; read images; and ask you to approve a step. Each machine decides what may run: only the programs you granted, or anything its own account can.

One row per call: the time, the account, the tool, the machine, the job and the outcome, each row chained to the one before by hash. Not the program's arguments and not its output: output passes through to your AI app, and the broker keeps it on your machine.

questions.q: Which systems can join a hub?
questions.a: Linux on x86_64 and ARM64, and Windows. macOS is coming.
No. There are no analytics or tracking scripts, and the broker and the MCP adapter make no network calls at all: the build refuses HTTP client libraries in them.
Any app that connects to a remote MCP server with OAuth: Claude on the web, desktop and phone, ChatGPT, Codex, Cursor, Gemini and others. They all use the same address.
Self-hosting runs on your own hardware, with no limit on calls. The hosted hub is free during its alpha.

claim.title: How claiming works

steps.term: The hub prints a claim link.
steps.text: A hub with no owner prints one to its own log each time it starts. Reading that log takes the server, or the platform its container runs on, so someone who only found the address cannot claim it.

steps.term: Open it where your passkey will live.
steps.text: On your phone or your computer. The code rides after the `#` in the link, which a browser never sends, so it stays out of every request and every log. You can also type the code in.

steps.term: Name the owner and make the passkey.
steps.text: One button does both, and you are signed in as the hub's owner.
It is deleted in the same step that stores your passkey, and from then on the hub refuses every claim.

paragraphs: The code is 120 random bits, and the hub keeps only its SHA-256. It works for a day; restarting the hub prints a new one, and only the newest works. A cancelled passkey prompt is retried with the same code.
claim.source: After that: add your machines from your account, and approve each AI app once with your passkey. The rest is in the [docs](/docs).

mcp.definition: Model Context Protocol: the open standard AI apps use to call tools on other systems. Your hub is one MCP server, at one address, for all of your machines.

passkey.definition: A sign-in key your phone or computer keeps and unlocks with your face, fingerprint or PIN. There is no password to steal, guess or reuse.

broker.definition: The {product} service on each machine. It runs what your AI asks as jobs it owns, under the machine's own {product} account, and keeps their output on the machine.

link.definition: The machine's one connection to your hub: a WebSocket the machine opens outward and keeps. Calls come down it, so the machine opens no port.

audit.definition: Every call is a row, and each row carries a hash of the row before it, so changing or deleting an old row breaks the chain where it happened.

oauth.definition: The standard way an app gets permission to act for you without your password. The app asks the hub, you approve it once, and it gets a token you can end.

digest.definition: The SHA-256 fingerprint of one exact container image. Pinned by digest, the hub runs precisely that build, not whatever a tag points at today.

claim-code.definition: A one-time code a hub with no owner prints to its own log. Reading the log takes the server, so only whoever runs the hub can claim it. It works for a day.
